lead: Stokes' theorem turns a line integral round a closed loop into a surface integral over any sheet that the loop bounds. The loop integral measures circulation; the sheet integral measures how much the field curls through the sheet. The two are equal. It exists because circulation and curl are the same idea seen at different scales. Engineers use it to compute work round a wing section, induced voltage round a circuit, and fluid swirl through a pipe mouth, often by swapping a hard integral for an easy one.
prereq: You need: curl from 6.2, line integrals from 6.4, surface integrals from 6.5, and the flat case from 6.6.

sections.h3: The statement and the right-hand rule

blocks.text: Take an open surface S: a sheet with a rim, not a closed bag. Give it a unit normal n at every point. Its boundary is a closed curve C. Orient C by the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of your right hand along C; your thumb points along n. Reverse C, and n flips too.

blocks.where: C is the closed boundary curve of the open surface S; F is a vector field with continuous partial derivatives; dr is a small step along C; ∇×F is the curl of F; n is the unit normal to S; dS is a small area element on S; the dot product (∇×F)·n keeps only the normal part of the curl.

blocks.text: The left side is a single integral along the rim. The right side is a double integral over the sheet. Both give the same number.

S may be curved, tilted, or wavy. Any surface that has C as its boundary gives the same right side. So you may replace a difficult sheet by a flat disk with the same rim. That freedom is the working power of the theorem.
The orientation rule links the two sides. Flipping n flips the sign of the surface integral. The matching flip of C flips the line integral. Both sides change together, so the equality survives.

sections.h3: Why a flat surface gives Green's theorem

blocks.text: Put S in the plane z = 0, so n = k. Write F = P i + Q j + R k with P, Q, R functions of x, y, z.

blocks.where: P, Q, R are the components of F, and each partial derivative is taken with the other two variables held constant.

blocks.text: On the flat sheet the normal is k, so only the k-component survives: (∇×F)·k = ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y. The area element is dS = dx dy. The surface integral becomes ∬<sub>D</sub> (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dx dy over the plane region D inside C.

On the same sheet dz = 0, so F·dr = P dx + Q dy. The line integral is ∮<sub>C</sub> (P dx + Q dy). Matching the two sides gives Green's theorem. Stokes' theorem is Green's theorem lifted off the plane onto a curved surface. The normal component of the curl is the local spin density through the sheet; adding it over the sheet gives the total circulation round the rim.

Two moves solve most problems. To evaluate a line integral ∮<sub>C</sub> F·dr on a nasty space curve, find any surface S with that curve as boundary, compute ∇×F, dot with n, and integrate over S. A flat disk or triangle is easiest. To evaluate a surface integral ∬<sub>S</sub> (∇×F)·n dS on a curved cap, replace the cap by a flat surface with the same boundary and integrate there.

items: Sketch S and C. Mark n and the direction of C using the right-hand rule.
Choose coordinates for S. A plane z = constant gives dS = dx dy; a disk in the xy-plane gives polar coordinates.
Dot the curl with n at each point before integrating. If n is constant and the curl is constant, the integral is just (∇×F)·n times the area.

blocks.text: The shortcut in step 4 is common in exams: a disk of radius 2 with curl (0, 0, 2) and n = k gives 2 × π(2²) at once.

figure.caption: The surface and its normal fix the boundary direction; the circulation round C equals the flux of the curl through S. The worked example uses a flat disk of radius 2 with n = k and C anticlockwise.

spec.title: Stokes' theorem and its orientation rule
spec.aria: A surface with its normal and boundary curve feeds a circulation integral that equals the flux of the curl, with an orientation link back to the start.

examples.question: Verify Stokes' theorem for F = (−y, x, 0) on the disk S: x² + y² ≤ 4 in the plane z = 0, with n = k and C the circle x² + y² = 4 traversed anticlockwise viewed from above.
steps: Write the components: P = −y, Q = x, R = 0.
The disk has radius 2, so its area is π(2²) = 4π ≈ 12.5664 square units.
Parametrize the boundary: r(t) = (2cos t, 2sin t, 0) with 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π, anticlockwise. Then dr = (−2sin t, 2cos t, 0) dt.
On C, F(r(t)) = (−2sin t, 2cos t, 0). So F·dr = (−2sin t)(−2sin t) + (2cos t)(2cos t) + 0 = 4sin²t + 4cos²t = 4.
examples.answer: Both sides equal 8π ≈ 25.1327, so Stokes' theorem holds for this field and disk.
examples.check:
import math
r = 2.0
area = math.pi * r * r
curl_z = 2.0
surface = curl_z * area
line = 4.0 * 2.0 * math.pi
print(round(area, 4))
print(round(surface, 4))
print(round(line, 4))

traps: Mismatching the orientation of C and n: reversing one side but not the other flips the sign of one integral only, so the two sides differ by a factor of −1.
Plugging n = k into a curved surface: on a tilted or curved sheet n changes from point to point, so write the local normal or switch to a flat surface with the same boundary.
Taking a component of F and then curling it: compute ∇×F first, then dot with n. The order matters because n may vary over S.
Applying Stokes' theorem to a closed surface such as a sphere: there is no boundary curve, and the closed-surface result is Gauss' theorem, not Stokes'.
Using a curve that is not the boundary of the chosen surface: the line integral must go round the rim of the same surface used on the right side.

quiz.q: State Stokes' theorem for an open surface S with boundary C.
quiz.a: ∮<sub>C</sub> F·dr = ∬<sub>S</sub> (∇×F)·n dS, where n is the unit normal to S and the direction of C is fixed by the right-hand rule.

quiz.q: Why may you replace a curved surface by a flat disk with the same boundary?
quiz.a: Both surfaces share the same boundary C, so both right-hand sides equal the same line integral. Stokes' theorem makes the surface integral independent of the chosen surface.

quiz.q: For F = (y, 0, 0), take S as the disk x² + y² ≤ 9 in z = 0 with n = k, and C the circle x² + y² = 9 anticlockwise. Find the surface integral of the curl.
quiz.a: Curl F = (0, 0, −1). Dot with k gives −1. Area = π(3²) = 9π. Surface integral = −1 × 9π = −9π. The line integral also gives −9π.

quiz.q: In the worked example, what goes wrong if you keep n = k but traverse C clockwise?
quiz.a: Clockwise C with n = k breaks the right-hand pairing. The line integral changes sign to −8π while the surface integral stays +8π, so the equality fails. Correct it by using n = −k or by reversing C.

quiz.q: For F = (0, x, 0), let S be the hemisphere x² + y² + z² = 4, z ≥ 0, and C its boundary circle. Compute the flux of ∇×F through S.
quiz.a: Curl F = (0, 0, 1). Use the flat disk of radius 2 in z = 0 with the same boundary. Dot with k gives 1. Area = 4π. Flux = 4π.

quiz.q: How does Stokes' theorem reduce to Green's theorem when S lies in z = 0 with n = k?
quiz.a: Then (∇×F)·k = ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y and dS = dx dy, so the surface integral becomes the double integral of Green's theorem. The line integral becomes ∮(P dx + Q dy).

quiz.q: Why is it wrong on a curved surface to take the k-component of F and then curl it?
quiz.a: The needed scalar is (∇×F)·n at each point, and n changes over a curved surface. Taking a fixed component first ignores the local normal, so the result is a different field and the integral is wrong.

beyond: Not for the exam. Stokes' theorem is the mathematical heart of Faraday's law: the voltage round a loop equals the rate of change of magnetic flux through any surface the loop bounds. In computational fluid dynamics, circulation round a blade section is computed from the curl of velocity through a nearby surface. Computer graphics uses the same identity in vorticity-based smoke animation. Search for 'Faraday's law Stokes theorem', 'vorticity flux', and 'discrete exterior calculus' to go further.
